title: Karmic tail 21-7-13 in the destiny matrix: the victor’s chariot and the unarmed rider

seo.title: 21-7-13 in the destiny matrix: the “Destroyer and Killer” karmic tail
seo.description: The 21-7-13 karmic tail is not about killing but about how a person ends things: with a cut or in peace. Date check, the loop and the way out per Waite and Wen.

short: 21-7-13 is the karmic tail that popular destiny matrix readings call “the Destroyer and Killer”. The name is louder than what lies behind it. The three cards of the tail — The World, The Chariot and Death — describe not a killing but the way a person ends things: projects, relationships, whole chapters of a life. The tail opens with the card of the finale and closes with the card of the end, and between them rides a victor. The loop goes like this: a person conquers their world, sees that it does not match the plan, passes sentence — and cuts: leaves in a single day, burns bridges, crosses people out. The task of the tail is Death in its old sense: not to kill, but to complete.

sections.h2: The one-minute check: the 21-7-13 tail has two sums — 13 and 49
paragraphs: A karmic tail is fixed entirely by one sum — the arcana of the day, month and year. The other steps of the formula only unfold it into three cards. Two sums lead to 21-7-13: 13 and 49. The second also reduces to 13 (4 + 9), so the rule can be put more briefly: if the sum reduces to 13, the tail is 21-7-13.

ol: **Day arcanum.** Your day of birth, if it is 22 or less. If it is more, add its digits: 23 → 5, 27 → 9, 31 → 4.
**Month arcanum.** The number of the month, from 1 to 12.
**Year arcanum.** Add the digits of the year; if the result is over 22, add its digits again: 1990 → 19, 1985 → 23 → 5.
**The sum.** Add the three numbers. If you get 13 or 49, the tail is 21-7-13.

paragraphs: Three examples. 03.05.1985: 3 + 5 + 5 = 13 — that is 21-7-13. 22.08.1990: 22 + 8 + 19 = 49 — so is this. But 01.02.1990 gives 1 + 2 + 19 = 22, and the tail comes out different, 3-7-22: The Chariot in the middle and Justice in the centre stay the same, but the entry and the root change. The sums 22, 31 and 40 give the same centre but lead to the tails 3-7-22 and 12-16-4.
Why exactly 13 and 49 work. From here the method’s formula runs the same way for everyone whose numbers fall like this:
This arithmetic gives facts shared by all 678 dates with this tail:

ul: **The centre is Justice.** Apart from 21-7-13, it sits in the centre of only two other tails out of 26: 3-7-22 and 12-16-4.
**Manipura is 8-8-16.** The chakra of standing, will and money reads the same for everyone: Justice, Justice and The Tower.
**Death is a root only here.** In none of the other 26 tails does 13 stand at the root. In the middle of a tail Death appears only once more, in 3-13-10.
**The World opens the relationship line.** Point M is the entry both of the tail and of the relationship line M–R1–R, so for everyone that line begins with The World.
**The energy of the two lower chakras is fixed:** for Svadhisthana (joy, children, creativity) it is 21, The World; for Muladhara (body, support, matter) it is 13, Death.

paragraphs: The formula gives 21-7-13 for 678 dates out of 46,299 between 01.01.1900 and 05.10.2026. That is twentieth place among the 26 possible tails: only six are rarer. Sex does not affect the numbers.

sections.h2: Where the name “Destroyer and Killer” comes from, and what is wrong with it
paragraphs: Popular sites retell one legend, sometimes with a sequel: “Destroyer and Killer. Death to many souls.” In a past incarnation the soul was supposedly a cruel person — an executioner, a jailer, a merciless fighter in wars and riots — and the cause of many deaths. Hence, the legend says, a hard present life and the task of saving lives: surgery, maternity wards, helping people on the edge. Some readings add a threat: whoever fails to work off the tail risks leaving before their time. None of this can be checked. A date of birth says nothing about past lives or about the length of this one, and there is no step in the method that would.

Yet the vocabulary of the name really does lie in the cards. Write out the divinatory meanings from Arthur Waite’s “The Pictorial Key to the Tarot” (1910), and the list for Death opens with the words **“End, mortality, destruction, corruption”**. Among the meanings of The Chariot are “war, triumph, presumption, vengeance”. The destroyer comes from Death; the warrior and the avenger come from The Chariot.
Still, the name gets the main thing wrong, for three reasons.

The first is frequency. The tail falls on roughly one birthday in 68: a school of a thousand pupils will have about fifteen of them. The portrait of an executioner does not fit that share of people. The tail describes something far more everyday.

The second is Waite himself. He called the skeleton with a scythe “the crude notion of the reaping skeleton” and replaced it in his deck with an apocalyptic horseman. Of that horseman he writes: **“The horseman carries no visible weapon”** — and yet “king and child and maiden fall before him”. A killer without a weapon is the exact formula of this tail. Whatever dies here does not die from a blow.

The third is what exactly dies. In 21-7-13 it is not people that fall but ties, projects and periods of life. A resignation letter written overnight. A move to another city instead of a conversation. A number on the block list. A company closed to spite a partner. And the phrase in which this tail is heard most clearly: “He’s dead to me.” That is the killing without a weapon — a sentence after which a person goes on living but vanishes from someone else’s life. A more accurate name for the tail would be not “the Destroyer” but “the Victor Who Cannot Finish”.

sections.h2: Two endings: the central riddle of the tail
paragraphs: The first and last cards of the tail are both about an end, but about different ends. What follows is about what Waite and Wen wrote about the cards; the cards on the site are its own drawings, and their details may differ.

Waite calls The World “this final message of the Major Trumps”: in tarot it is the finale of a journey that begins with The Fool. In the matrix The Fool takes the number 22, but the finale is still The World. Waite writes that the card represents **“the perfection and end of the Cosmos”**. Benebell Wen, in “Holistic Tarot” (2015), opens her reading with the words “fulfillment, completion, and triumph in all undertakings”. This is the end as a summit: the work is done, the circle is closed, the wreath can go on.

Death is the thirteenth card, and Waite’s divinatory list for it opens with one word: “End”. Two words later stands “destruction”. This is the end as a break: the work is not finished, it has been stopped.

The 21-7-13 tail stands between these two endings. At its entry is completion; at its root, a break. And the whole question of the tail is which of the two endings a person chooses when something in their life is coming to an end.

The World has one more detail, unexpected for a final card. Waite writes that it is **“perhaps more especially a story of the past”** — of “that day when all was declared to be good”. For a tail that the matrix reads as a memory of the past, the detail is telling: The World at the entry is a picture of how everything should be when all is good. Against that picture a person measures everything they later conquer. Wen adds that when The World appears in the past position, it suggests “the state that is predetermined or outlined for the Seeker”, though whether the Seeker reaches it “is to be determined by present conditions and choices”. The picture of the whole is given. The whole is not.

There is also a third possibility, and Waite wrote it down too. The reversed meanings of both cards begin with the same word — **“Inertia”**. For The World it goes on: “fixity, stagnation, permanence”. For Death: “sleep, lethargy, petrifaction, somnambulism; hope destroyed”. When an ending can be neither completed nor broken off, it freezes. There are no reversed cards in the matrix — a calculated number does not lie upside down — but these lists show where a card’s quality turns when it stops working.
So the tail has three outcomes for any ending:

ul: **Complete** — The World: carry it through, admit that it is done, leave in peace.
**Break off** — Death as destruction: the cut, the escape, the burned bridges.
**Freeze** — the inertia shared by both cards: living in something that ended long ago.

paragraphs: The popular name sees only the second outcome. But the tail is built so that the first is always close by: The World stands at its entry. **The destroyer is the one who breaks off what could have been completed.**

sections.h2: The King in his triumph and the death of Kings: what links The Chariot and Death
paragraphs: Between the two endings stands The Chariot, and Waite describes it in a way that makes its link to the root of the tail visible without any interpretation.

In the first part of his book Waite writes of The Chariot: **“it is really the King in his triumph”** — and uses the Latin currus triumphalis, the triumphal chariot. Of Death the same part says that in its current and patent meaning it is **“more especially a card of the death of Kings”**. The mechanism of the tail is the King in his triumph. Its root is the death of Kings. Wen sees the same in Death: for someone of high status the card is a reminder that “no one is above suffering”, and here the king is equal to the peasant.

People joined this pair — triumph and mortality — long before tarot. Tertullian, in his “Apology” (around 197 AD), writes of the Roman triumph: even on that loftiest of chariots the general is reminded that he is a man — from behind him comes the prompt: **“Look behind you! Remember that you are a man”** (Respice post te! Hominem te memento!). The familiar “memento mori” is a later retelling of the same scene. A similar rite was kept for centuries at the coronation of the popes: the procession was stopped three times, a bundle of flax was burned before the new pope, and a voice said: “Holy Father, thus passes the glory of the world.” The glory of the world is almost word for word the entry of the tail, and it passes the way things pass at its root.

For 21-7-13 this leads to a simple conclusion: the tail needs a voice at its back. The Chariot itself does not hear that voice, and Waite explains why. The charioteer, he says, is “conquest on all planes—in the mind, in science, in progress”. But then comes a list of caveats, and the main one is this: **“the planes of his conquest are manifest or external and not within himself”**. The liberation he brings to others “may leave himself in the bondage of the logical understanding”. The Chariot knows how to take the world from the outside. On the inside, nothing in it ever gets completed.

Plutarch preserved a story that shows this better than any card. Alexander the Great, hearing from the philosopher Anaxarchus that there was an infinite number of worlds, wept: “Is it not worthy of tears that, when the number of worlds is infinite, we have not yet become lords of a single one?” The popular version — “he wept because there were no more worlds to conquer” — turns the meaning upside down. In Plutarch the conqueror weeps because his world will never be whole. That is The Chariot before The World: every victory turns out to be not a whole but one more piece.

Wen adds a trait to the portrait of The Chariot that explains how such a victor ends things. He likes to appear in control, but has **“a tendency to run from his or her problems (or attack the problems with such aggression as to subdue it and therefore avoid true, mature confrontation)”**. Two ways to end things — escape and rout. Both bypass a third: the conversation, the settling of accounts, the goodbye. Exactly the kind of ending that is called The World.

sections.h2: The arithmetic of the tail: The World is Death that has passed through the scales
paragraphs: The numbers of the tail are calculated from one another, and in 21-7-13 the sums read almost like instructions.

ul: **13 + 8 = 21.** The entry M is the root plus the centre. Death laid on the scales of Justice gives The World: an ending that has been honestly weighed becomes a completion.
**13 + 21 = 34 → 7.** The mechanism N is the root plus the entry. An ending together with completeness gives The Chariot: a new road opens once the old one is closed.

paragraphs: This is our reading of the method’s arithmetic, not a statement by Waite or Wen. But it shows exactly where the tail’s way out lies. Between the break and the whole stand the scales. Take them away, and Death remains just Death.

The scales are the centre of the chart, its comfort zone: the state a person returns to when nothing is happening. For everyone with 21-7-13, Justice sits there. Waite gives it the meanings “Equity, rightness, probity” and **“triumph of the deserving side in law”**. The word “triumph” appears in the descriptions of three cards out of four: for The Chariot in Waite — “war, triumph”; for Justice — “triumph of the deserving side”; for The World in Wen — “triumph in all undertakings”. The fourth card, Death, begins with the word “End”. The 21-7-13 tail is three promises of victory and one word that sums them up.

The subtlety is in which court is meant. Wen stresses that Justice is “human-made justice, not divine justice”. And she describes its reverse side: aggression, “blind enthusiasm in a particular cause that may bring more harm than good”, actions prompted by the feeling of having been treated unfairly — when in fact everything was fair. In 21-7-13 the scales almost always serve one purpose: to present the ending as deserved. “He brought it on himself”, “they never valued me here”, “this is only fair”. The sentence is passed in a private court, and that court has no defence.

One more consequence of the arithmetic shows in the chakras. Manipura, the chakra of standing, will and money, reads 8-8-16 for everyone with this tail: Justice, Justice and The Tower. A verdict added to a verdict gives lightning. Waite describes The Tower as “the ruin of the House of Life, when evil has prevailed therein”, and more precisely as the fall of **“a House of Falsehood”**, recalling the psalm: “except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Ps. 127:1). Wen writes that The Tower often appears in readings for “the cutthroat ambitious, for those who embody the combination of ambition, ego, pride, and talent”. 3-7-22 and 12-16-4 have the same Manipura; it is a property of the centre, not of one tail. But in 21-7-13 it lies on top of Death at the root: the theme of collapse is woven not only into the old scenario but also into the way a person builds a career and money.

sections.h2: How the loop turns: picture, victory, verdict, the cut
paragraphs: The best portrait of 21-7-13 in Russian literature was written by Pushkin. “The Song of Wise Oleg” (1822) opens with the destroyer’s formula: “Wise Oleg is gathering now / To take revenge on the foolish Khazars; / For their wild raid he has doomed / Their villages and fields to the sword and the fire.” Revenge comes from Waite’s list for The Chariot, “doomed” is a word of judgment, and sword and fire are the destruction from the list for Death. The Chariot, Justice and Death in four lines.

Then a soothsayer foretells the prince’s fate, and the prophecy runs exactly in the order of the tail. First The World: “Thy name is made glorious by victory; / Thy shield hangs on the gates of Tsargrad; / The waves and the land bow down to thee.” Then The Chariot — the horse which, “sensing its master’s will”, now stands calm under the enemy’s arrows, now races across the field. And at the end, Death: **“But thy death shall come from thine own horse.”** The end will come from the very thing that carries him to victory.

The most interesting part is what Oleg does. He does not argue with the ending; he cancels it: he dismounts, says goodbye and orders the horse to be led away. “And another horse was led up to the prince.” Years later, at a feast, he asks about the old horse and learns that it died long ago. The prince rides out to look at its bones, laughs at the prophecy — and the end catches up with him right there, beside what he had sent away and forgotten. Pushkin was writing about a fate that cannot be cheated. For the 21-7-13 tail, something else in the ballad matters more: **what has been removed from a life without being completed does not disappear — it lies on the hill and waits**.
The loop goes through six steps:

ol: **The picture of the world.** The entry — The World. The person carries an image of the whole: what a family, a career, a friendship, a project should be. Not a dream but a standard against which everything else is measured. Most often in an “all or nothing” format.

**Victory.** The mechanism — The Chariot. Will, drive, speed: the person gets what they set out for — the job, the person, the market. Conquest comes to them more easily than anything, and others remember them that way.

**The crack.** The conquered world turns out to be alive and does not match the picture: the partner is an ordinary person, the business is routine, the top of the career is the same meetings. The Chariot does not know how to live in what it has conquered. Its business is to drive on.
**The verdict.** The centre — Justice. The scales switch on: “this is not what I fought for”, “he doesn’t deserve it”, “this is only fair”. The trial is held alone and fast.

**The cut.** The root — Death in its crude sense. An ending in a single evening: the letter of resignation, the move, the block list, “he’s dead to me”. Or escape without explanation — The Chariot’s second way, according to Wen. No conversation, no settling of accounts, no goodbye.
**A new horse.** Relief, freedom, a new road — and the same picture of the world ahead. Unfinished endings are left behind, and with every round there are more of them.

paragraphs: The most vulnerable point of the loop lies between the fourth and fifth steps, when the sentence has been passed but not yet carried out. While a decision is still only a decision, it can be turned into a completion: talk it through, finish the work, pay the debts, say goodbye. What makes it dangerous is speed.

Here is how it looks in ordinary life. Ten years of friendship. A friend does not come to the opening of the business that the person with this tail has lived for over the last two years. By evening the chat history is deleted, the number blocked, and mutual friends have been told: “He no longer exists for me.” Why the friend did not come, the person never found out: the defence was given no word in this court. The trial took an evening, the sentence a minute. A year later the person notices that they think of that friend more often than when they were friends.

sections.h2: The other pole: a world turned to stone
paragraphs: If you read only the popular descriptions, 21-7-13 seems always to be the one who wrecks things. But The World and Death share a reverse side — inertia — and the tail can be lived from that side. Wen describes reversed Death almost as a portrait: the Seeker feels stuck or inert, **“feels like nothing has been accomplished”**, is disappointed “due to the inability to let go and move on”, and “the Seeker’s resistance to change is the source of the pain”. Of reversed The World she writes that the Seeker “is afraid of change and is hesitating”, and sometimes “is consciously and knowingly in denial” about what is happening in their life.
There are at least three such variants.

**The keeper of ruins.** A job that has long been pointless. A relationship in which there has long been no one. A business that brings neither money nor joy. All of it is held together not by love but by an inability to put a full stop. Waite’s “petrifaction” is not a metaphor here but a description of ordinary days.

**The one who waits for someone else to end it.** They cannot make an ending with their own hands, so they steer someone else towards it: they cool off, withdraw, provoke — until the partner or the boss says “enough”. The cut happens anyway, only the axe is in someone else’s hands.

**Long patience and one day.** Most often the poles alternate. For years the person lives in something that has died, and then in a single day tears everything down — including what was still alive. Others see a destroyer. The person remembers the years when they could not end anything.

Both poles have the same way out — the root of the tail, Death in its real meaning. For the destroyer it is the ability to slow down and complete. For the petrified, it is the ability to begin an ending at all.

The most visible price of 21-7-13 shows after ten or fifteen years. There is no one around from earlier chapters of life: no old friends, no former colleagues to recommend them, no calm relations with exes. Every new world is built from zero, because nothing was carried out of the old one. The victor turns out to be a person with no home front.

The second price is that the unfinished does not disappear. Like the bones of Oleg’s horse, it lies where it was left and makes itself felt at the worst moment: in longing for what was abandoned, in the same conflict with a new partner, in the same exit from a new job. A scenario that has not been completed gets repeated.

The third price is written in Manipura: The Tower. Standing and money often grow fast for someone with this tail — The Chariot knows how to take — and collapse just as fast, sometimes by their own hand. A business is closed not because it fails but because it is “not on the right scale”. A career is wiped out by a door-slamming exit. People remember how they left, not what they did.
For someone living at the pole of inertia, the price is the mirror image — years. Time lived in a world that ended long ago.

sections.h2: How the 21-7-13 tail shows up in life
paragraphs: Below are typical scenes, not predictions. The tail describes a habitual course, not what is bound to happen.

paragraphs.h3: Relationships: The World stands at the entry twice

paragraphs: Point M — the entry of the tail — also serves as the entry of the relationship line M–R1–R. So for everyone with 21-7-13, the first card in closeness and the first card in the old scenario are the same — The World. Relationships begin with a picture of the whole: “us”, a shared home, a story forever. The conquest is the brightest phase: The Chariot knows how to win someone. Then the partner turns out to be a separate person with a life of their own, the scales start counting, and the couple ends either in a single evening or in a long cooling, when both spend years living in a petrified “us”.
The relationship line of this tail always begins with The World but never repeats the whole tail. In 21-7-13 the old scenario and the way of loving start from the same card and then go separate ways.
The strong version of this scene is a person who knows how to part humanely and is therefore not afraid to stay. When an ending stops being a catastrophe, there is no need to run.

Justice, Justice, The Tower. At work this often gives a rare ability — to close. Projects, divisions, loss-making branches, negotiations that drag on. Where others drag out for years what does not work, the person with this tail sees the end before anyone else and is not afraid to name it.

The shadow is the same ability without the scales. Firing someone “as a lesson to the rest”, shutting a project down a week before it pays off, breaking with a partner in the heat of the moment, walking out of a business at the cost of one’s share — anything to leave today. For 411 of the 678 people with this tail, or 61%, The Tower also stands in the social purpose — the point that shows how a person is useful to many; for the other 267 it is The Chariot. A repeated arcanum is not doubled by repetition, but it shows that in such a chart the theme of destruction and rebuilding goes beyond the tail, and its strong version can become a calling.

Popular readings advise this tail to take up professions that save lives: surgery, maternity wards, helping people in crisis. The cards give grounds for something broader — work in which ending is part of the job. Crisis management and restructuring, bankruptcy and winding up companies, editing where half the work is striking things out, rescue services, demolition and reconstruction, supporting people through divorce, inheritance and loss. Wen writes that Death is traditionally related to “death and birth, property and inheritance, society and family, war and treaties”. These are examples, not a prediction of a profession.

paragraphs.h3: Moving: a change of place as a way to end things

paragraphs: Waite’s divinatory list for The World contains words unexpected for a card of completion: **“voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place”**. For 21-7-13 geography is part of the scenario. The fastest way to end everything at once is to leave: a new city, a new country, new people, and no one will ask how the past ended.

A move in this tail can be the completion of a chapter, or an escape from it. The difference is easy to see. Completion is when, before leaving, every word has been said, every debt paid and every task handed over. Escape is when the departure is the only word.

For a parent with this tail, a child growing up is the main exam, because childhood is an ending too, and the one that can least be cancelled. The Chariot wants to steer, and popular readings have good reason to advise this tail not to run their children’s lives. The loop can turn both ways here. One can cut: “if you’re so grown up, live on your own”, and shut the door on the day of the first serious argument. One can freeze: go on deciding for a thirty-year-old the way one decided for a ten-year-old, because the end of childhood was never acknowledged.
The version that works lies in between: notice that one stage has ended and say so out loud — in words, not with a slammed door.

sections.h2: Completion or destruction: telling them apart by the cards
paragraphs: The same card can work in two ways in this tail. The words in the table come from Waite’s divinatory lists and descriptions; the split into “loop” and “strength” is ours.

head: Card and role
When the loop is turning
When the strength is working
rows: “all or nothing”, flight and a change of place instead of a conversation; or fixity, stagnation
**assured success, recompense**: see it through and admit that it is done
war, presumption, vengeance; escape or rout instead of an honest confrontation
**succour, providence**: a will that carries others rather than crushing them
destruction, a break in a single evening; or inertia, petrifaction
**rebirth, renewal**: an ending with a road after it
a sentence passed in a private court, bias, excessive severity

paragraphs: Four questions help to see where a person is right now:

ul: **What is ending?** A person or a project — or only my picture of them?
**How long does the ending take?** One evening is a cut. Weeks with a conversation are a completion.
**Who heard about the ending?** Found out after the fact — a cut. Said face to face — a completion.
**What is left afterwards?** Scorched earth and blocked numbers — the loop. Meeting in the street and saying hello — The World.

sections.h2: What changes the scenario: nine practices
paragraphs: Waite’s horseman of Death **“moves slowly”**. Half the answer lies in that detail: an ending done well is not a blow but a passage that has time. Wen calls the appearance of Death “a call to let go of the present and move on” — to let go, not to destroy. The practices below add to the tail what The Chariot lacks: a pause, words and a voice at its back.

ol: **Get a voice at your back.** The Roman general in triumph heard “remember that you are a man”. What is needed is a person given the right in advance to say “stop” — a friend, a mentor, a partner. Any decision about a big ending — leaving, breaking up, closing a business — is first said out loud to them.

**Ride slowly.** A decision to end something, made today, is announced no sooner than a week later. If a week later it is the same, it is not a flare-up but a decision, and it can be carried out calmly.

**Separate the world from the picture.** Before the verdict, write down what exactly is wrong — the person themselves, the work itself, or the fact that they did not match my image? Many cuts end at this question.

**End with words.** Every ending comes with a conversation: what was good, what did not work, what I am taking with me. Even a short one. This is the “true, mature confrontation” that The Chariot, according to Wen, avoids.
**Listen for “he’s dead to me”.** It means the sentence has been passed without a defence. Replacing it with “we are no longer close” means ending without killing anyone.

**Hand things over.** When leaving a job, a project, a city — hand things over as if you might come back: pass them on, explain, say thank you. In Waite The World means “recompense”, and it goes to the one who saw things through.

**Clear one set of ruins.** Pick one burned bridge and complete it: a letter, a call, a returned debt, a “thank you” said at last. Not to restore it, but to close it. The bones of the horse are better buried than walked around.

**Set a deadline.** This is for the pole of inertia: set a date by which whatever is no longer alive will be either changed or ended — and keep it. The Chariot’s will in the service of Death, not against it.

**Celebrate completions.** Mark the ends of stages: a project delivered, a chapter closed, a child grown up. The World’s wreath is put on after the outcome, not before the battle. A victory without a celebration of completion quickly turns into the next war.

paragraphs: If thoughts of death stop being a metaphor — about your own life or someone else’s — that is not a question for the destiny matrix. In danger, call your local emergency number. Psychologists and crisis lines work with such thoughts, and you can turn to them at any moment.

sections.h2: The strong version of 21-7-13: the one who knows how to end wars
paragraphs: The tail holds a hint that only shows in Russian. Arcanum 21 is called Mir, and in Russian that word means both the universe and a life without war. Before the spelling reform of 1918 they were two different words: “міръ”, the universe or society, and “миръ”, the absence of war. Tolstoy titled his novel “Война и миръ”, War and Peace, setting peace against war; half a century later Mayakovsky answered with the poem “Война и міръ”, War and the World. The tarot card is mir in the first sense, the whole. But in 21-7-13 The World stands next to The Chariot, and in Waite’s list for The Chariot, right after “succour, providence”, comes “war”. War and mir meet in one triple — in both senses.

This is a play of the language, not Waite’s. But it describes the strong version of the tail exactly. Death, in Wen, is traditionally related among other things to “war and treaties”, and the end of a war is a treaty. **The strong 21-7-13 is not the one who never destroys, but the one who knows how to end wars — their own and other people’s.**

Such a person can be recognised by a few signs. They can close a project everyone is afraid to close — and do it so that people leave grateful. They leave without enmity and keep the doors open behind them. They finish what others abandoned halfway. In a crisis they calmly say “this is over” and lead people through the transition instead of running or smashing. They are not afraid of endings — so they need neither escape nor rout.

All of this is written in the same lists, only on the front side. For The World — **“Assured success, recompense”**. The list for The Chariot does not begin with war at all but with “Succour, providence”. For Justice — “Equity, rightness, probity”. And of Death Waite writes that its existing explanations — “rebirth, creation, destination, renewal” — are, on the whole, better than usual.

One last detail is about what the unarmed horseman carries. In Waite it is a black banner emblazoned with the Mystic Rose, and the rose, in his words, **“signifies life”**. Ahead, between two pillars on the verge of the horizon, shines the sun of immortality. Wen adds that the rider and horse are marching towards the rising sun, though that sun is still far in the distance. The path of 21-7-13 runs from an ending that cuts to an ending that carries the banner of life. The destroyer remains the same person with the same power to end things. What changes is only what is left behind: scorched earth — or peace.
Six other tails are easy to confuse with 21-7-13: they share the entry, the middle, the centre, or have Death among their cards.

paragraphs: The most instructive pair is 21-7-13 and 3-7-22. Both tails have The Chariot in the middle and Justice in the centre, and both have the same Manipura. But they drive in opposite directions. 3-7-22 is a tail of beginnings: from The Empress, who gives birth, to The Fool, who takes the first step. 21-7-13 is a tail of endings: from The World, where the road has been travelled, to Death. The same chariot carries some to the start and others to the finish.

Permutations — 13-7-21, 7-21-13, 21-13-7 and others — are never produced by the tail formula for any date. If such a triple turns up in a reading, it belongs to another position in the chart or to another school of calculation, and it cannot be read as 21-7-13.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: **Calculation.** The classic destiny matrix by Natalia Ladini’s method: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M, with every sum reduced to 22 or below. The “sum of 13 or 49” rule and all the statistics come from going through every date from 01.01.1900 to 05.10.2026 — 46,299 days.

**Waite.** A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, 1922 reprint): the descriptions of The World, The Chariot, Death, Justice and The Tower from parts one and two, and the divinatory meanings from part three. Quotes are given in Waite’s original wording.
**Wen.** Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015), the sections on The World, The Chariot, Death, Justice and The Tower. Quotes are given in Wen’s original wording.

**Literature and history.** A. S. Pushkin, “The Song of Wise Oleg” (1822), quoted in our translation; Tertullian, “Apology”, chapter 33; Plutarch, “On Tranquillity of Mind”, chapter 4, in the Loeb translation; the papal coronation rite with the words “Sic transit gloria mundi”, first recorded in 1409; L. N. Tolstoy, “War and Peace”; V. V. Mayakovsky, “War and the World” (1916).
**The Bible.** Ps. 127:1 (Ps. 126:1 in Russian numbering) — as the source of the verse Waite quotes.

**Our reading.** The three outcomes of an ending, the reading of the arithmetic (13 + 8 = 21, 13 + 21 → 7, 8 + 8 = 16), Oleg as a portrait of the loop and the play on the word “mir” are the author’s interpretation, not statements by Waite or Wen. The past-life legend is given as a popular interpretation, not as fact.

paragraphs: In compatibility, 21-7-13 can be read as the task of changing a shared route in time while respecting different paces of adjustment. The World at M concerns ambitious plans and openness to new experiences; the Chariot at N develops the task through how goals are pursued; Death at D raises the question of ending an outgrown stage and accepting change. This is our interpretation using Lisovskaya’s pair positions, rather than a ready-made account from her book.

A shared venture may have stopped bringing satisfaction after many decisions were made for its sake. One person wants to close it; the other proposes simply working harder. The Chariot’s capacity to follow through can then keep the couple travelling a route that no longer serves their shared dream. The World helps reveal other possibilities, provided something new does not become a demand to erase everything that came before.

Name precisely what is ending: a particular project, a way of earning, or a familiar routine. Separate that from what you want to preserve between you, then divide the practical work of closing the stage. The difficulty is forcing a partner to change faster or treating every ending as defeat. A transition with clear steps helps this combination: acknowledge what has been done, settle commitments, and choose a small next experience that both people accept.

faq.q: What happened in a past life to someone with the 21-7-13 tail?
faq.a: The popular legend speaks of a cruel person who caused many deaths: an executioner, a jailer, a merciless fighter. This cannot be checked: a date of birth holds no information about past lives. The legend works as a metaphor for the scenario “conquer and destroy”, but not as a biography.

faq.q: Does Death in the tail mean an early death or danger to life?
faq.a: No. A calculated number says nothing about the length of a life or about misfortunes, and the threat of “leaving before your time if you don’t work off the tail” is intimidation, not method: there is no step in the calculation that would say so. Waite himself called the skeleton with a scythe a crude notion and considered the explanations “rebirth, renewal” better than usual. Death at the root of the tail is a task — learning to end things — not a forecast.

faq.q: Is the 21-7-13 tail different for women and men?
faq.a: The numbers are the same: sex plays no part in the calculation. Popular readings say that men with this tail travel a path from harshness to wisdom, while women go through scenarios of loss and submission. More likely the difference lies in what kind of ending people around allow: some are more easily forgiven a cut, others only long patience. The loop is the same either way: picture, victory, verdict, ending.

faq.q: Should someone with this tail become a surgeon or a rescuer?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The advice to “save lives” grew out of the legend of atonement. The cards of the tail speak of a different skill — ending things and leading people through a transition. A surgeon needs it, and so do a crisis manager, an editor and the parent of a teenager. The profession here is an example, not a prescription.

That is sometimes what people call the karmic tail itself. This triple has no other place in the matrix: going through every date since 1900 shows that 21-7-13 never falls on the relationship line, the money line or the talent line, or in the chakras. If the triple is called a programme, it still means the tail.

faq.q: Can the 21-7-13 tail be “closed” or “worked off”?
faq.a: The numbers of a date do not change; the tail stays in the chart for good. What changes is how it is lived: the loop “victory — verdict — the cut” opens up when time and words appear between the decision and the ending. The measure is not a feeling of “I’ve worked through it” but the fact that one can calmly say hello to people from earlier chapters of life.

ul: **Cards and roles:** 21 The World — entry, 7 The Chariot — mechanism, 13 Death — root. Everyone with this tail has the same arcanum in the centre of the chart — 8, Justice.
**How to tell from a date:** the arcana of the day, month and year add up to 13 or 49. Both sums reduce to 13, and there is no other way to this tail.
**How often:** 678 dates out of 46,299 since 1900, or 1.46% — roughly one birthday in 68.
**The main trap:** not cruelty but an ending without a goodbye — sentence and break in a single evening.
**The way out:** end things slowly and all the way, so that every war is followed by peace.

report: Arthur Waite’s horseman of Death **“carries no visible weapon”**. Waite called the skeleton with a scythe “the crude notion of the reaping skeleton” and took it out of his deck. And yet the 21-7-13 tail, with this horseman at its root, goes by “the Destroyer and Killer” in popular readings.

A legend explains the name by a past life: the soul was supposedly an executioner, a jailer, a merciless fighter, and the cause of many deaths. None of this can be checked — a date of birth says nothing about past lives. Yet the vocabulary of the name really does lie in the cards. Waite’s divinatory list for Death opens with “End, mortality, destruction”. Among the meanings of The Chariot are “war, triumph, presumption, vengeance”. Only, what dies in this tail is not people but ties, projects and whole chapters of a life. A resignation letter written overnight. A move instead of a conversation. A number on the block list. And the phrase in which the tail is heard most clearly: “He’s dead to me.” That is the killing without a weapon.

report.h3: The King in his triumph and the death of Kings

report: Waite wrote down the link between the middle of the tail and its root himself. Of The Chariot he says: “it is really the King in his triumph”. Of Death: “more especially a card of the death of Kings”. The Romans joined the two long before tarot. Tertullian tells how a general riding in triumph was prompted from behind to look back and remember that he was only a man.

The Chariot itself does not hear that voice. Its conquests, in Waite’s words, are **“manifest or external and not within himself”**: it knows how to take the world from the outside, but on the inside nothing in it ever gets completed. Benebell Wen adds how such a victor ends things. He likes to appear in control, but tends to run from problems — or to attack them so hard that he subdues them and avoids “true, mature confrontation”. Escape or rout. Both bypass a third way — the conversation, the settling of accounts, the goodbye.

report.h3: Two endings, and a third that freezes

report: The tail opens with the card of the finale and closes with the card of the end. Waite calls The World “the perfection and end of the Cosmos” — the end as a summit: the work is done, the circle is closed. Death is the end as a break: the work is not finished, it has been stopped. Between them rides a victor.

There is a third outcome as well. In Waite, the reversed meanings of The World and of Death begin with the same word — “Inertia”: fixity, stagnation, petrifaction. When an ending can be neither completed nor broken off, it freezes. Hence the tail’s second pole: years in a job that has long been pointless and in a relationship where there has long been no one, and then everything torn down in a single day — including what was still alive.
The popular name sees only the break. But The World stands at the entry of the tail, which means that **the destroyer is the one who breaks off what could have been completed.**

The best portrait of this loop was written by Pushkin. “The Song of Wise Oleg” opens with the destroyer’s formula: the prince is setting out “to take revenge on the foolish Khazars” and has “doomed” their villages “to the sword and the fire”. Revenge, sentence, destruction. The prophecy runs exactly in the order of the tail: first The World — “The waves and the land bow down to thee”, then the horse that carries him to victory, and at the end — “But thy death shall come from thine own horse.”

Oleg does not argue with the ending. He cancels it: he dismounts and orders the horse to be led away. “And another horse was led up to the prince.” Years later the end catches up with him beside the bones of what he had sent away and forgotten. For 21-7-13, this is what matters most in the ballad: what has been removed from a life without being completed does not disappear — it lies on the hill and waits.

The loop turns like this. First comes a picture of the whole — what a family, a career, a project should be. Then victory: conquest comes to this tail more easily than anything. Then the crack: the conquered world is alive and does not match the picture. The scales switch on — everyone with this tail has Justice in the centre of the chart: “he brought it on himself”, “this is only fair”. The sentence is passed in a private court, with no defence. And the ending comes in a single evening. Then a new horse, the same picture ahead and new ruins behind. The price shows ten years on: no one is left from earlier chapters of life, and unfinished scenarios repeat themselves with new people.

The arithmetic of the tail points to the way out. The entry of the tail is the root plus the centre: 13 + 8 = 21. In our reading, Death laid on the scales gives The World. An ending that has been honestly weighed becomes a completion. And Waite’s horseman of Death **“moves slowly”**: an ending done well is not a blow but a passage that has time.

Hence the practices. Find a voice at one’s back — a person given the right in advance to say “stop”. Announce a decision about a big ending no sooner than a week later. End with words: what was good, what did not work, what I am taking with me. Listen for “he’s dead to me” and replace it with “we are no longer close”. Pick one burned bridge and close it — with a letter, a call, a returned debt. Not to restore it, but to close it.

The last hint only shows in Russian. Mir, the Russian name of arcanum 21, means both the universe and a life without war, and Waite’s list for The Chariot includes “war”. **The strong 21-7-13 is the one who knows how to end wars — their own and other people’s.** Such a person closes the project everyone is afraid to close, leaves without enmity, and leads people through a transition instead of running or smashing. In Waite the unarmed horseman carries a black banner with a rose, and the rose, in his words, “signifies life”. The destroyer remains the same person with the same power to end things. What changes is only what is left behind: scorched earth — or peace.

If thoughts of death stop being a metaphor — about one’s own life or someone else’s — this is not a question for the destiny matrix. In danger, call a local emergency number or crisis line; psychologists and crisis services work with such thoughts.
